reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: Hereditary distal RTA reflects a failure of the distal nephron to secrete hydrogen ions, producing a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis
The hallmark biochemical clue is an inappropriately alkaline urine (pH persistently high) despite systemic acidosis
Hypokalaemia is characteristic and can cause muscle weakness, and profound hypokalaemia may precipitate paralysis or arrhythmia
Chronic acidosis mobilises bone buffer, causing hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia and consequent nephrocalcinosis and stone formation
Autosomal recessive forms (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) are often associated with sensorineural hearing loss and present early; autosomal dominant SLC4A1 disease is generally milder
Children may present with failure to thrive, rickets and polyuria, whereas adults may present with stones, osteomalacia or unexplained hypokalaemia
Alkali replacement (for example potassium citrate or bicarbonate) corrects the acidosis, replaces potassium and raises citrate to limit nephrocalcinosis
reference.pathophysiology: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis arises from impaired hydrogen ion secretion by the alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Inherited forms result from mutations affecting the apical H+-ATPase (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) or the basolateral chloride-bicarbonate exchanger AE1 (SLC4A1). Because the distal nephron cannot generate a steep enough pH gradient, net acid excretion falls and a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis develops with inappropriately alkaline urine. Persistent acidosis drives calcium out of bone, raises urinary calcium and lowers citrate, promoting nephrocalcinosis and stones, while potassium wasting produces hypokalaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis and Fanconi syndrome
Type 4 (hyperkalaemic) renal tubular acidosis from hypoaldosteronism
Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss from chronic diarrhoea
Acquired distal RTA from Sjogren syndrome or other autoimmune disease
Toxin- or drug-induced distal tubular dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate and calculation of a normal serum anion gap
Simultaneous urine pH and assessment of urinary anion gap or ammonium excretion
Ammonium chloride or furosemide-fludrocortisone acidification testing where diagnosis is unclear
Renal ultrasound or CT for nephrocalcinosis and stones
Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss
Targeted genetic testing of SLC4A1, ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle paralysis or cardiac arrhythmia
Failure to thrive or rickets in an infant or young child
Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function
Obstructing stone with infection requiring urgent intervention
reference.prognosis: With sustained alkali and potassium replacement, growth, bone health and biochemistry usually improve and stone or nephrocalcinosis progression slows, though established nephrocalcinosis and chronic kidney impairment may persist.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not measuring urine pH during systemic acidosis, when it should be inappropriately high
Overlooking associated hearing loss in recessive forms
Attributing the hypokalaemia to diuretics or diarrhoea rather than tubular loss
Correcting acidosis with sodium bicarbonate alone and worsening hypokalaemia by not replacing potassium
management: Lifelong oral alkali replacement with sodium bicarbonate or potassium citrate to correct the hyperchloraemic acidosis and reduce bone buffering
Potassium supplementation, preferably as potassium citrate, to correct hypokalaemia while simultaneously raising urinary citrate
Potassium citrate to reduce hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia and thereby limit nephrocalcinosis and stone formation
Treat established bone disease (rickets or osteomalacia) with alkali therapy alongside vitamin D and calcium as needed
Monitor electrolytes, acid-base status and growth in children, with renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and stones
Audiometry and hearing support for the sensorineural deafness of recessive forms
Genetic counselling and family screening for SLC4A1, ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 variants
Nephrology referral, with urgent attention when profound hypokalaemia threatens paralysis or arrhythmia
